skills.name: Describe the physical and chemical properties of sulphur and its allotropes

note.text:
Sulphur is a brittle yellow solid, insoluble in water, soluble in carbon disulphide, and a poor conductor of heat and electricity.
Allotropes are different forms of the same element in the same physical state. Sulphur has two crystalline allotropes:
• Rhombic (alpha) sulphur: octahedral crystals, stable below about 96 °C, density 2.07 g/cm³.
• Monoclinic (beta) sulphur: needle-shaped crystals, stable between about 96 °C and the melting point, density 1.98 g/cm³.
96 °C is the transition temperature. Plastic sulphur, a brown rubbery form made by pouring boiling sulphur into cold water, is not crystalline and slowly changes back to rhombic sulphur.
Chemically, sulphur burns in air with a blue flame to sulphur dioxide, and combines with many metals on heating to form sulphides.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text:
By the end, you should be able to describe the properties of sulphur and tell its allotropes apart by crystal shape, stability and density.
Builds on: Lesson {1} (where sulphur comes from) and Form Three structure and bonding.
Leads to: Lessons {3} to {8}, which deal with the compounds sulphur forms.

sections.heading: Physical properties and allotropes
sections.text:
Sulphur is a brittle yellow solid. It is insoluble in water, dissolves in carbon disulphide, does not conduct electricity, and melts at about {115} °C.
Allotropes are different forms of the same element in the same physical state. Sulphur has two crystalline forms:
• Rhombic (alpha): octahedral crystals, density {2.07} g/cm³, stable below about {96} °C. Grown by letting carbon disulphide evaporate from a solution of sulphur.
• Monoclinic (beta): needle-shaped crystals, density {1.98} g/cm³, stable between about {96} °C and the melting point. Grown by letting molten sulphur cool slowly and pouring off the liquid left.
About {96} °C is the transition temperature, where one form changes into the other.

mistake.wrong: rhombic and monoclinic sulphur are isotopes of sulphur
mistake.why: Isotopes differ in the nucleus. Allotropes differ in how the same atoms are arranged.

worked_example.problem: A sample of sulphur is kept at {t - 20} °C for several days and then at {t + 10} °C for several days. Name the stable form in each case.
steps: Below {t} °C the stable form is rhombic (alpha) sulphur, with octahedral crystals.
Between {t} °C and the melting point the stable form is monoclinic (beta) sulphur, with needle-shaped crystals.
{t - 20} °C is below {t} °C, and {t + 10} °C is above it.

cards.idea: Allotropes are different forms of the same element in the same state.
example: rhombic and monoclinic sulphur are both pure solid sulphur

cards.idea: Rhombic sulphur is stable below about {96} °C; monoclinic above it.
Sulphur burns in air with a blue flame to give sulphur dioxide.

pick.q: Sulphur is heated in a deflagrating spoon and lowered into a gas jar of air. What is seen and formed?
pick.r: A blue flame, forming sulphur dioxide, {formula('SO2')}
w: A yellow flame, forming sulphur trioxide, {formula('SO3')}
A white flame, forming a white solid
Nothing happens
e: {formula('SO3')} is made in the Contact process with a catalyst, not by burning sulphur in air.
The product is a gas, not a solid.
Heated sulphur burns in air with a clearly visible flame.
pick.y: S + {formula('O2')} → {formula('SO2')}, with a blue flame and a choking smell.

pick.q: Iron filings and sulphur are heated together. What is formed?
w: A mixture of iron and sulphur, unchanged
Iron(II) sulphate, {formula('FeSO4')}
Iron and sulphur dioxide
e: Heating makes them react; the product cannot be separated with a magnet.
No oxygen is present, so no sulphate can form.
No oxygen is present, so no {formula('SO2')} can form.
pick.y: Fe + S → {formula('FeS')}: sulphur combines with many metals when heated.

pick.q: What does sulphur do with dilute hydrochloric acid?
pick.r: Nothing: sulphur does not react with dilute acids
w: It gives off hydrogen
It gives off hydrogen sulphide
It dissolves to give a yellow solution
e: Only metals above hydrogen give off hydrogen with a dilute acid.
That happens with a metal SULPHIDE, not with sulphur itself.
Sulphur is insoluble and unreactive towards dilute acids.
pick.y: Sulphur reacts with hot concentrated acids, but not with dilute ones.

pick.q: Why is a deflagrating spoon used to burn sulphur in a gas jar?
pick.r: It holds the burning sulphur safely in the jar while the gas collects
w: It makes the sulphur burn more brightly
It stops the sulphur from melting
It dries the gas as it forms
e: The brightness depends on the sulphur and the air, not on the spoon.
The sulphur melts before it burns; the spoon holds the molten sulphur.
The spoon does not dry anything.
pick.y: The long handle lets the burning sulphur be lowered into the jar and taken out safely.

pick.r: Different forms of the same element in the same physical state
w: Different elements with the same properties
Compounds of one element with another
Atoms of one element with different numbers of neutrons
e: Allotropes are forms of ONE element, not different elements.
No other element is joined: an allotrope is still the pure element.
Those are isotopes, which differ in the nucleus, not in the arrangement of the atoms.
pick.y: Rhombic and monoclinic sulphur are both pure solid sulphur, with the atoms packed differently.

pick.q: Which allotrope of sulphur is stable below {96} °C?
w: Monoclinic (beta) sulphur
Plastic sulphur
Both are equally stable
e: Monoclinic sulphur is the stable form between about {96} °C and the melting point.
Plastic sulphur is not stable at all: it slowly changes back to rhombic.
Only one form is stable at a given temperature.
pick.y: Below the transition temperature of about {96} °C, rhombic sulphur is the stable form.

pick.q: What shape are the crystals of monoclinic sulphur?
w: Octahedral crystals
Cubes
It has no crystals at all
e: Octahedral crystals are the rhombic form.
Neither allotrope of sulphur forms cubes.
Monoclinic sulphur does form crystals; it is plastic sulphur that has none.
pick.y: Monoclinic sulphur grows as needles, while rhombic sulphur grows as octahedral crystals.

pick.q: In which liquid does sulphur dissolve?
w: Water
Dilute hydrochloric acid
Ethanol, very readily
e: Sulphur is insoluble in water.
Sulphur does not react with or dissolve in dilute acids.
Sulphur is only very slightly soluble in ethanol.
pick.y: Sulphur is insoluble in water but dissolves well in carbon disulphide, which is how rhombic crystals are grown.

pick.q: What is seen when sulphur burns in air?
pick.r: A blue flame, giving a colourless gas with a choking smell
w: A bright white flame, giving a white solid
A yellow flame, giving a black solid
No reaction takes place
e: A bright white flame with a white solid is burning magnesium.
A black solid is not formed; the product is a gas.
Sulphur burns readily when heated in air.
pick.y: Sulphur burns with a blue flame to give sulphur dioxide: S + {formula('O2')} → {formula('SO2')}.

pick.r: By pouring boiling sulphur into cold water
w: By cooling molten sulphur very slowly
By dissolving sulphur in carbon disulphide and evaporating
By heating sulphur gently to just above its melting point
e: Slow cooling gives crystals, not the plastic form.
That method grows rhombic crystals.
Gentle melting gives a runny amber liquid, which sets back to a crystalline form.
pick.y: Sudden cooling traps long chains of sulphur atoms, giving a brown rubbery solid that is not crystalline.

questions.prompt: Which form of sulphur is stable at {t} °C?

distractors.text: Neither: sulphur is liquid at that temperature

misconceptions.explain: Rhombic is stable BELOW about {96} °C and monoclinic above it, up to the melting point.
Plastic sulphur is never the stable form: it slowly changes back to rhombic.
Sulphur melts at about {115} °C, so at {t} °C it is still solid.

solution: {t} °C is {t < 96 ? 'below' : 'above'} it, and the melting point is about {115} °C.

pick.q: Rhombic and monoclinic sulphur are both pure sulphur, yet their densities and crystal shapes differ. Why?
pick.r: The same atoms are packed in a different arrangement in each crystal
w: They contain different numbers of neutrons
One of them contains a little oxygen

e: Different numbers of neutrons give isotopes, which have the same crystal forms.
Both allotropes are pure sulphur; neither contains oxygen.
Allotropes are forms of ONE element, not different elements.

pick.r: It slowly changes into rhombic sulphur, the stable form below {96} °C

It melts
e: Below the transition temperature the monoclinic form is not stable.

pick.r: By dissolving sulphur in carbon disulphide and letting the liquid evaporate slowly

By pouring boiling sulphur into cold water

e: Sulphur is insoluble in water, so no solution can be made.
That gives plastic sulphur, which has no crystals.
Heating alone does not grow crystals.

w: It takes in oxygen from the air
It loses water
It reacts with the carbon dioxide in air
